passage:
Naveen, I swear, Farhan sir hates me. Every time I send him something he replies in one line: 'Fine.' 'Fix slide 4.' 'Noted.' No hello, no thanks. With the other interns he jokes, but with me it's all business. So I just keep my head down in meetings and don't say anything. Why give him more to dislike?
Then yesterday Rimjhim told me he'd asked her, 'Is Sanjana even interested in this role? She never asks a single question.' Interested? I'm staying back till eight!
I thought quiet meant respectful. He thinks it means I don't care. And I thought short meant he hates me. Maybe it just means he's drowning in emails, like everyone. I don't know.

qa.q: How late does Sanjana say she is staying back?
qa.a: She is staying back till eight.

qa.q: Why has Sanjana been keeping her head down in meetings?
qa.a: She believes Farhan sir dislikes her because of his one-line replies, so she stays quiet to avoid giving him more reasons.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Sanjana now that she knows how her silence looks?
qa.a: She could ask a question or two in the next meeting, or tell Farhan sir she is keen to learn, so he stops reading her silence as lack of interest.

qa.q: How does Farhan sir seem to see Sanjana's silence?
qa.a: He seems to read it as lack of interest, not realising she is quiet out of respect and fear, and he may not notice how brisk his replies sound.

grounding: A woman intern reads her male senior's brisk replies as dislike while he reads her silence as disinterest.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, and I sit between Bidisha's desk and Mr Rao's cabin at the accounts firm, so I see both sides. Mr Rao talks to everyone in bullet points: 'Ledger. Today. Thanks.' He doesn't mean anything by it; he's been like that for fifteen years. But Bidisha, who joined in June, flinches every time. She's stopped asking him anything and just quietly guesses. Last week in the tea room Mr Rao said to me, 'That new girl doesn't seem very interested. Never asks a thing.' The same afternoon Bidisha whispered, 'He can't stand me, can he?' I didn't know what to tell either of them. I think they're both wrong. Nobody explains, and nobody asks.

qa.q: When did Bidisha join?
qa.a: Bidisha joined in June.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's whisper 'He can't stand me, can he?' reveal about how she reads Mr Rao?
qa.a: She takes his brisk bullet-point style as personal dislike, and she seems anxious and hurt by it.

qa.q: How could someone like Lakshmi gently help at this stage?
qa.a: She could tell Bidisha that Mr Rao talks this way to everyone and encourage her to ask, or mention to him that the new joiner may need more explanation.

qa.q: How does Mr Rao see Bidisha's quietness?
qa.a: He reads her silence as lack of interest, not realising his short style has made her afraid to ask.

grounding: A colleague sees a senior read a new woman's silence as disinterest while she reads his brisk tone as dislike.

passage:
So here's the funny part, looking back. In my first month at the firm, Pankaj sir barely said anything to me except things like "Fine" or "Send it by five." I decided he disliked me. Honestly, I was sure of it.
So I, the only girl in that team, stopped talking in the huddles. I just nodded and took notes.
Then at the end of the month he said to someone, not knowing I could hear, "Manjula doesn't seem very interested. Never asks anything."
I was shocked. Not interested? I was terrified! And he wasn't disliking me, he was just like that with everyone, short and quick, because he had twelve projects.
We'd each made up a story about the other. That's me, Manjula. Quiet does not mean bored, I learnt.

qa.q: How many projects did Pankaj sir have?
qa.a: Twelve projects.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she overheard Pankaj sir's comment?
qa.a: She was shocked and hurt, because she had actually been terrified, not uninterested.

qa.q: What turning point could fix this kind of misreading?
qa.a: One of them checking the story, for example Manjula asking how she is doing, or Pankaj sir asking her opinion in a huddle.

qa.q: What is Pankaj sir experiencing as he judges Manjula's silence?
qa.a: He likely feels mildly disappointed, reading her quiet as a lack of interest, while too busy to notice she is scared.

grounding: Shows an intern reading her senior's brisk tone as dislike while he reads her silence as lack of interest.

passage:
Week 1: Vasudha joined the design studio. Omkar, her lead, spoke in quick half-sentences. "Colours, too many. Fix." Vasudha went home thinking, He doesn't like me.
Week 2: In reviews, Vasudha stopped offering ideas. She did exactly what was asked, silently. Omkar told a colleague over coffee, "The new intern doesn't seem that into it."
Week 3: The colleague mentioned it to Vasudha, gently. Vasudha stared. "Not into it? I'm scared of him." That afternoon she stayed after the review and said, "Omkar, I'm very interested. I just thought you found me annoying." Omkar blinked. "Annoying? I talk like this to everyone."

qa.q: What did Omkar say about the colours?
qa.a: "Colours, too many. Fix."

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling in week two when she stopped offering ideas?
qa.a: She felt hurt and scared, believing Omkar disliked her, so she kept quiet to stay safe.

qa.q: What turning point did Vasudha reach in week three?
qa.a: She named the misreading directly, telling Omkar she was interested and had thought he found her annoying.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when he hears he seemed to dislike her?
qa.a: He is probably surprised and a bit embarrassed, realising his brisk style was taken personally.

grounding: Shows an intern reading her lead's brisk tone as dislike while he takes her silence for lack of interest, until she names it.

passage:
Nirmala, come, I'll tell you about my worst mistake as a manager. It was 2004, at the bank. I had a new trainee, a quiet young woman. She never spoke in meetings. I thought, this one doesn't care.
I was busy, you see. I spoke to everyone in short bursts. "Do this. Wrong. Again." I didn't think about it.
Three months later she asked for a transfer. Her letter said she felt I disliked her from day one. Disliked her! I'd been planning to recommend her for the analyst track. Her work was careful.
She was reading my tone, and I was reading her silence, and we were both wrong. So remember this from your old Naveen uncle: explain your feedback, and ask the quiet ones what they think.

qa.q: What did the trainee ask for after three months?
qa.a: A transfer.

qa.q: What might young Naveen have felt when he read her letter?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and regretful, realising she felt disliked while he had been planning to recommend her.

qa.q: In the story, what choice could Naveen have made earlier?
qa.a: Explaining his feedback and asking the quiet trainee what she thought, instead of assuming her silence meant she didn't care.

qa.q: What was the trainee experiencing during those three months?
qa.a: She felt disliked and probably anxious, taking Naveen's brisk tone personally and staying silent to protect herself.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he read a trainee's silence as lack of interest while she read his brisk tone as dislike.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof of the site office, and Arvind had to half-shout every instruction. "Measurements by noon. Check the east wall again." Simran nodded and wrote it down, saying nothing. Arvind watched her head stay bent over the notebook and thought, she never asks a single question; maybe she doesn't care about this work at all. Across the table, Simran heard only the clipped words and the sigh at the end. He can't stand me, she decided. At lunch she ate alone in the jeep, while he told the foreman the new intern seemed checked out. Neither of them mentioned that the roar of the rain had swallowed half of what was said, or that he had been on the phone with an angry client since seven that morning.

qa.q: Where were Simran and Arvind working that morning?
qa.a: In the site office, while rain hammered its tin roof.

qa.q: What did Simran feel when she heard Arvind's clipped words?
qa.a: She felt hurt and anxious, deciding he could not stand her, though his tone came from the noise and the angry client.

qa.q: What could either of them do to break the misreading?
qa.a: Arvind could explain what the recheck is for, and Simran could ask one question, which would show her interest and test her guess.

qa.q: How does Arvind read Simran's silence?
qa.a: He takes it as a sign she does not care about the work, when she is actually taking careful notes.

grounding: Shows a senior reading a new worker's silence as lack of interest while she reads his curt tone as dislike, with neither checking.
